City of London · Urban walks

The City of London dragon walk: follow the boundary most people miss

White dragons stand guard where the City begins. Link them together and a familiar business district turns into a walk through boundaries, lost gates and stubborn fragments of old London.

By Paolo Pastorino27 September 20266 min read
At a glance
Start
Temple Bar or London Bridge for a shorter section
Distance
Flexible; split the western and eastern sections
Allow
2 hours for a section; half a day for a broad circuit
Cost
Free

Most people enter the City of London without noticing the moment it happens. The traffic continues, the buildings barely pause and there is no wall to cross. Look up, however, and a white dragon may be clutching a red-and-white shield above the road.

These boundary markers turn an administrative line into a physical walking route. Following them is less about collecting every statue than learning where the City ends, why certain streets matter and how much history hides in places designed for movement.

Why dragons guard the City

A pair of dragons has supported the City’s shield in its coat of arms since the early seventeenth century. The boundary markers seen today were installed at important entry points, many in the late twentieth century, each dragon holding the heraldic shield.

They are often mistaken for griffins. The wings, claws and reptilian body make the City’s intended creature clear, even if heraldry is not your usual hobby. Once you recognise the silhouette, the markers become difficult to unsee.

The grandest examples announce major approaches; smaller dragons perch on columns beside roads that have lost their ceremonial importance. Together they describe a border that remains legally meaningful even where it feels invisible at street level.

A route, not a treasure hunt

There is no single compulsory order. A satisfying western section begins near the Temple Bar dragon on Fleet Street, continues around the Temple and Victoria Embankment, then turns towards Blackfriars and the north-western edge of the City. An eastern section can pick up markers around Aldgate, Bishopsgate and the approaches to London Bridge.

Trying to join every dragon in one outing creates a long, stop-start walk. Splitting the circuit into west and east gives more time for the places between them: Smithfield, St Bartholomew the Great, the Barbican, Spitalfields, riverside lanes and the remains of streets shaped by former gates.

Use the dragons as punctuation rather than the entire story. A marker beside a six-lane road may not be beautiful, but it tells you that this precise crossing once deserved a formal welcome.

The details worth noticing

Look at the direction each dragon faces and the form of its base. Some stand alone as monuments; others seem to have been squeezed into modern street furniture. The repeated shield creates continuity, while differences in scale reveal which entrances the City wanted to make ceremonial.

The surroundings are equally important. At London Bridge, the boundary aligns with one of the City’s oldest approaches. Near Temple, legal London presses against financial London. Around Aldgate and Bishopsgate, the names of vanished gates survive even when the structures do not.

This is also a good walk for spotting the City’s smaller obsessions: plaques fixed high on walls, parish boundaries, old ward names and pieces of architecture preserved at improbable angles beneath newer buildings.

Planning the walk

Wear comfortable shoes and expect diversions. Construction, security barriers and traffic crossings can make the most direct line unpleasant. A map is useful, but do not treat a missing dragon as failure: some markers are easy to pass when trees, buses or road signs block the view.

Weekends reduce commuter pressure, although parts of the City become very quiet and cafés close earlier. Weekdays provide more life but demand patience at busy junctions. Early morning offers the cleanest photographs.

For a shorter version, choose three or four markers and connect them with one strong destination: One Leadenhall terrace, the Barbican, St Bartholomew the Great or the riverside. The route works best when the dragons lead somewhere rather than becoming the only purpose.

What the walk changes

The City is often described vertically through towers and viewpoints. The dragons make you read it horizontally, along its edge. Streets that seem unrelated begin to form a perimeter, and names such as Aldgate or Bishopsgate recover their literal meaning.

The dragons do not reveal a lost wall. They reveal how often we cross a boundary without asking who drew it.

By the end, the creatures themselves may be less interesting than the habit they teach: look above traffic height, question official symbols and pay attention whenever London quietly announces that one place has become another.
